fields.title: Grace Abounding (For Teens)
fields.description: Before he wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress, John Bunyan was a young tinker who swore so badly that a woman at a neighbour’s shop told him he could spoil a whole town, then a churchgoer who was secretly proud of it, then a man tormented for years by thoughts he hated and could not stop. This teen edition retells his own story of doubt, fear and rescue: the voice in the middle of a game, the women talking in the sun, the words “Sell Him” and the verse that pulled him out, told straight and in plain words, with what it means if your own head is a hard place to live.

qa.question: What is Grace Abounding?
qa.answer: It is John Bunyan’s own account of how he came to faith, written in prison in 1666. It tells his inner story honestly: the years of guilt, doubt, frightening thoughts and false starts, and the Bible verses that finally brought him peace. The Pilgrim’s Progress tells much the same journey as an allegory.

qa.question: Who was John Bunyan?
qa.answer: A tinker, a mender of pots and pans, born at Elstow near Bedford in England in 1628. He served in the army at sixteen, married at about twenty, joined a church in Bedford, and became a preacher. In 1660 he was arrested for holding unlawful religious meetings and refusing to conform to the Church of England, and spent twelve years in prison, where he wrote this book.

qa.question: Why is this book good for teenagers?
qa.answer: Because Bunyan is honest about the things many young people go through and rarely say out loud: doubting whether God is real, fearing you have gone too far, being proud of looking good, and having thoughts in your head that you hate. He shows how God met him in all of it.

qa.question: What does “Sell Him” mean in the book?
qa.answer: For about a year a thought kept pushing into Bunyan’s mind, telling him to “sell” or give up Christ for anything at all. One morning, worn out, he felt his heart give way to it, and for two years afterwards he was sure he had committed the unforgivable sin. Much of the book is about how God showed him he had not.

qa.question: How did Bunyan find peace in the end?
qa.answer: Through particular Bible verses that he held on to, above all “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” and “My grace is sufficient for thee.” The turning point came in a field, when he saw that his righteousness was Jesus Christ himself in heaven, not his own good or bad moods.

qa.question: Is this the full text?
qa.answer: No. It is a retelling for teenagers in plain modern words, keeping Bunyan’s own sentences where they say it best. The full Grace Abounding is also available.

qa.question: What if I struggle with thoughts like Bunyan’s?
qa.answer: You are not alone and you are not beyond God’s reach. Bunyan found that having a thought he hated was not the same as choosing it. If frightening or unwanted thoughts keep forcing themselves on you, tell a trusted adult, a pastor or a doctor. Help is real and it works.

fields.title: The Voice in the Middle of the Game
fields.body_html:
“Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.” — Job 21:14 (KJV)

John Bunyan was born in 1628 in Elstow, a village near Bedford in England. His father was a tinker, a man who mended pots and pans, and his family was, in his words, “of that rank that is meanest and most despised of all the families in the land.” He went to school just long enough to learn to read and write, and then, he admits, he “did soon lose that little I learned.”

By his own account he was a ringleader. He says he had few equals “for cursing, swearing, lying, and blaspheming the holy name of God.” Even so, at nine or ten he had terrifying dreams about devils and the day of judgment. They scared him, but they didn’t change him. When the dreams faded, he went straight back to what he enjoyed.

He nearly died more than once. He fell into a creek of the sea and was almost drowned. He fell out of a boat into the river at Bedford. He once stunned an adder with a stick, forced its mouth open and pulled out its sting with his fingers. As a soldier, he was about to go to a siege when another man asked to take his place. That man was shot in the head while standing guard, and died. Bunyan noticed all of this. None of it woke him up.

Then one Sunday the parson preached against breaking the Sabbath with sports and games, and Bunyan felt, for the first time he could remember, what guilt was. He went home with “a great burden upon my spirit.” By the end of his dinner it had worn off, and he was glad. That afternoon he was out playing a game called cat, a street game played with a stick and a small piece of wood, when this happened:

“A voice did suddenly dart from heaven into my soul, which said, Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?”

He stopped, stick in hand, and looked up. He felt as if Jesus were looking down at him, displeased. And then a second thought arrived, the one that would follow him for years: it is too late. Christ won’t forgive you now. His reasoning went like this: “I can but be damned, and if I must be so, I had as good be damned for many sins, as to be damned for few.” So he went back to the game, and for about a month he threw himself into sin as hard as he could.

Look at that second thought carefully, because it is one of the oldest lies there is. It sounds honest. It sounds like facing facts. But it was not God’s voice. God’s question had been an offer: will you leave your sins and come? The voice that said “too late, so you might as well” came from somewhere else. Bunyan later said this kind of despair, the quiet feeling that “there is no hopes for them,” is more common than many people realise.

If you have ever thought, “I’ve already messed up too much, so what’s the point?”, you are standing exactly where Bunyan stood in the middle of that game. The rest of this book is about how wrong that thought turned out to be.

One thing to do this week: notice if a “too late, so what’s the point” thought shows up in you this week, about God, school, a friendship or a habit. When it does, say it out loud or write it down, and then write next to it: “That’s not the voice that invites me.”

study_questions.question: What question did Bunyan hear during the game of cat?
study_questions.answer: “Wilt thou leave thy sins and go to heaven, or have thy sins and go to hell?”

study_questions.question: Why did he go back to his sins after hearing it?
study_questions.answer: Because a second thought told him it was already too late, so he might as well be damned for many sins as for few.

study_questions.question: Why might “it’s too late, so why bother” be a lie rather than honesty?
study_questions.answer: Because God’s question was an invitation to come, not a closed door. Despair dresses itself up as facing facts, but it contradicts the offer God actually made.

fields.title: A Poor Painted Hypocrite
fields.body_html:
“For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7 (KJV)

The first thing that actually changed Bunyan was not a sermon. It was an embarrassing moment at a neighbour’s shop window. He was standing there “cursing and swearing, and playing the madman,” as usual, and the woman inside, whom he describes as no saint herself, told him she trembled to hear him. He was, she said, “the ungodliest fellow for swearing that ever she heard in all her life,” and could “spoil all the youth in a whole town.”

He hung his head. He wished he could be a little child again and learn to talk without swearing. He was sure he couldn’t change. And yet, he says, “how it came to pass, I know not,” from that day he stopped. He found he could talk better without the oaths than with them.

Around the same time he had married. He and his wife were so poor they came together “not having so much household stuff as a dish or spoon betwixt us both,” but she brought two Christian books her father had left her, and they sometimes read them together. Bunyan started going to church twice a day. He met a man who talked about the Bible, and he began to read it, though mostly the stories; Paul’s letters bored him. He tried to keep the Ten Commandments, felt good when he managed, felt bad when he didn’t, and promised to do better.

His neighbours were amazed. Bunyan, of all people, had become religious. They praised him to his face and behind his back. And here is the honest part: he loved it. “Though, as yet, I was nothing but a poor painted hypocrite, yet I loved to be talked of as one that was truly godly. I was proud of my godliness.” He did this for about a year, and later said that if he had died then, “my state had been most fearful.”

There is a strange, almost funny story from this stage. Bunyan had loved bell-ringing at the church. Now he decided it was too worldly, so he stopped, but he still went to watch. Then he started to worry that a bell might fall on him, so he stood under a beam. Then he worried a falling bell might bounce off the wall and hit him anyway, so he stood in the doorway. Then he worried the whole steeple might fall, and he ran away.

That is what religion feels like when it is built on fear and performance: you keep moving to a safer spot, and nothing ever feels safe. Bunyan had changed his behaviour a great deal. But he hadn’t met Jesus. He later wrote that he was “all this while ignorant of Jesus Christ, and going about to establish my own righteousness.”

It is possible to become the “good kid” at church, at school or among your friends, and quietly enjoy the reputation more than you love God. Being better behaved is good. Being admired for it is pleasant. Neither one is the same as being forgiven.

One thing to do this week: think of one area where you are mostly managing how you look: to parents, friends, leaders, or in what you post. Do one good thing this week that nobody will see or praise. Notice how it feels when there’s no audience.

study_questions.question: What made Bunyan stop swearing?
study_questions.answer: A woman at a neighbour’s shop told him he was the worst swearer she had ever heard and could spoil all the young people in the town. He was ashamed, and from that day, to his own surprise, he stopped.

study_questions.question: Why did Bunyan call himself “a poor painted hypocrite”?
study_questions.answer: Because his life looked much better on the outside, and he loved being praised as godly, but he still did not know Jesus Christ and was trying to earn God’s approval by his own goodness.

study_questions.question: What does the bell-ringing story show about fear-based religion?
study_questions.answer: That trying to feel safe by keeping rules leaves you always looking for a safer spot. Bunyan kept moving further away and still never felt safe.

fields.title: Three or Four Poor Women
fields.body_html:
“Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.” — Matthew 7:14 (KJV)

Bunyan’s work as a tinker took him to Bedford, and one day he passed “three or four poor women sitting at a door in the sun, and talking about the things of God.” By now he thought of himself as quite good at religious conversation, so he drew near to listen. He understood almost none of it.

They were talking about being born again, about what God had done in their hearts, about how they had seen how bad they really were, and how God had “visited their souls with His love in the Lord Jesus.” They talked about their own unbelief and temptations. And, strangest of all to him, they talked about their own good deeds as worthless for earning anything. Bunyan wrote: “methought they spake as if joy did make them speak.” They seemed to him like people who had found a new world.

His heart began to shake. All his religion, he realised, had never once included the new birth. He kept going back to listen. He found two new things in himself: a soft, tender heart, and a mind that wouldn’t stop thinking about what he had heard. He began to read the Bible differently, and Paul’s letters, which had bored him, became “sweet and pleasant.”

He also lost friends. There was a young man called Harry whom he had loved more than anyone, but Harry’s life was all cursing and worse, and Bunyan stepped away from him. When they met again, Bunyan asked him what would become of him if he died like that. Harry answered: “What would the devil do for company, if it were not for such as I am?” Another religious friend turned to the Ranters, a movement that said nothing was sin any more, and laughed at him. Bunyan prayed, “Lord, I am a fool, and not able to know the truth from error: Lord, leave me not to my own blindness.”

Then came a picture that stayed with him. He saw, “in a dream or vision,” those Bedford women sitting on the sunny side of a high mountain, warm and happy, while he shivered in snow and cloud on the other side of a wall. He searched for a way through and at last found a tiny gap. He pushed and strained, got his head in, then “by a sidling striving, my shoulders, and my whole body,” and sat down with them in the sun.

He worked out what it meant. The mountain was the church; the sunshine, God’s kindness; the wall, God’s Word; and the narrow gap was Jesus Christ, the way to the Father. The gap was so tight, he said, that there was “only room for body and soul, but not for body and soul, and sin.”

Notice who God used. Not a famous preacher. A few women, poor and unnamed, chatting on a doorstep in the sunshine about what Jesus had done for them. They had no idea a future world-famous writer was listening. Your ordinary, honest talk about God may be the most important sermon someone ever hears.

One thing to do this week: have one honest conversation this week about what God is actually doing in your life, not just what you think about church. Keep it real, even if it’s small: a prayer answered, a doubt, a verse that helped.

study_questions.question: What did the women in Bedford talk about that Bunyan had never understood?
study_questions.answer: Being born again, God’s work in their hearts, seeing their own sinfulness, the love of God in Jesus, and how their own goodness could not save them. They spoke as if joy made them speak.

study_questions.question: What did the gap in the wall stand for in Bunyan’s vision?
study_questions.answer: Jesus Christ, the way to God the Father. It was so narrow that there was room for a whole person, but not for a person and their sin.

study_questions.question: Why is it significant that God used ordinary women chatting on a doorstep?
study_questions.answer: It shows that honest, everyday talk about what God has done can reach people far more than we realise. They had no idea who was listening.

fields.title: And Yet There Is Room
fields.body_html:
“And the servant said, Lord, it is done as thou hast commanded, and yet there is room.” — Luke 14:22 (KJV)

Wanting God did not make Bunyan feel safe. It made him anxious. Two fears hit him one after the other.

The first was: what if I’m not one of the chosen? He read that salvation is “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy,” and it felt like a locked door. A voice seemed to say, “It may be you are not,” and then, “you had as good leave off, and strive no further.” Some days the fear made him so weak he could hardly walk.

Then a sentence came into his head: “Look at the generations of old and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was confounded?” It was as if someone said: start at Genesis, read to Revelation, and find one person who trusted God and was let down. He was so encouraged he went home to look it up. He couldn’t find it. He asked Christian friends; nobody knew where it was. For more than a year he searched. In the end he found it in Ecclesiasticus, in the Apocrypha, not in the Bible itself. But by then he had seen enough of God’s kindness to know the thought was true anyway. It was, he said, “the sum and substance of many of the promises.”

The second fear was worse: what if it’s too late? What if the day of grace has passed? He imagined that the Bedford Christians were all the people God would save in that area, and that he had arrived after the door closed. “Oh, that I had turned sooner! Oh, that I had turned seven years ago!” He was so worn out he could hardly take another step. Then these words broke in, from Jesus’ story of the great supper: “Compel them to come in, that my house may be filled,” “and yet there is room.”

Bunyan took those words personally. He believed that when Jesus said them, he was thinking of people like him, people who would one day be terrified there was no place left. “There was place enough in heaven for me,” he wrote.

Around this time he finally told the Bedford Christians how he felt, and they introduced him to their pastor, Mr. Gifford, who invited him home to listen to people talk honestly about God. But being taken seriously made his struggles feel worse, not better. He began to see how much was wrong in his own heart, and he felt further from God than ever. His friends told him God’s promises; he said they might as well have told him to “reach the sun with my finger.”

Here’s the thing worth knowing: struggling after you start taking God seriously is normal. It is not proof that it isn’t working. Bunyan felt worse precisely because he had started to look honestly. And when the fear said “no room,” Jesus had already answered it, centuries before: and yet there is room.

One thing to do this week: if you have a fear about God that keeps coming back (Am I really his? Is it too late? Have I gone too far?), write it down. Then write under it, “And yet there is room,” and tell one Christian you trust about it. Don’t carry it alone like Bunyan did for months.

fields.title: My Love
fields.body_html:
“Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair.” — Song of Solomon 4:1 (KJV)

For a long time, Bunyan says, he was so disgusted with himself that he envied animals. Birds, fish and beasts, he thought, had no sinful nature and no soul to lose. He would gladly have swapped places with any of them. He was sorry God had made him a human being at all.

Then one day he heard a sermon on a single phrase from the Song of Solomon: “my love.” The preacher made five points: that a saved soul is Christ’s love even when it is unlovely; that Christ loves without a cause; that he loves when the world hates; that he loves under temptation and when God seems absent; and that he loves from first to last. Bunyan got nothing out of most of it. But on the fourth point the preacher said: when you are tempted, and God seems to hide his face, “yet think on these two words, My love, still.”

Walking home, Bunyan asked himself sourly, “What shall I get by thinking on these two words?” And then the words started to repeat inside him: “Thou art my love, thou art my love,” twenty times over, getting stronger and warmer each time. He kept answering, “But is it true, but is it true?” Then came the phrase from Paul: nothing “shall separate thee from my love.”

For the first time he really believed his sins could be forgiven. He was so full of joy he felt he could have preached God’s mercy “even to the very crows that sat upon the ploughed lands before me.” He wished he had a pen and ink right there, “for surely I will not forget this forty years hence.”

His next sentence is one of the most honest in the whole book: “but alas! within less than forty days, I began to question all again.”

Soon after, another verse began to ring in his ears: “Simon, Simon, behold Satan hath desired to have you,” Jesus’ warning to Peter. It sounded so loud that once he actually turned round, thinking someone half a mile behind him had shouted. Looking back, he realised it was a warning that a storm was coming. At the time, he didn’t understand.

If you’ve had a moment when God felt incredibly close, and then weeks later it felt like it never happened, you’re not weird and you haven’t lost it. Bunyan had his crows-on-the-field moment and lost the feeling in under forty days. Feelings come and go. The words didn’t change: “Thou art my love.” The love was true on the day he doubted it, just as it was on the day he felt it.

One thing to do this week: write down one time you felt God was real or close: a moment, a verse, a prayer. Date it. Keep it somewhere you’ll find it. Bunyan wished for pen and ink; you have them. On a flat day, read it again and remember that God hasn’t changed.

fields.title: Thoughts He Hated
fields.body_html:
“And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself.” — Colossians 1:20 (KJV)

About a month after that warning, the storm hit. Bunyan called it “twenty times worse than all I had met with before.” First his comfort disappeared. Then darkness. Then “whole floods of blasphemies,” thoughts against God, Christ and the Bible, poured into his mind. Was there really a God? Was the Bible just a clever story? Every religion thinks it’s right, so how could he know his was?

Much worse than the questions were the thoughts themselves. Ugly, blasphemous words would “bolt out” of his heart whenever he heard God mentioned. In church, in prayer, while reading the Bible, the thoughts came. Sometimes he felt pushed to say terrible things about God out loud, and he was so afraid of doing it that he would “clap my hand under my chin, to hold my mouth from opening.” He thought he might be going mad, or that the devil had taken him over.

This lasted about a year. Here is a detail that matters: in the middle of it all, Bunyan noticed something. “By the distaste that they gave unto my spirit, I felt there was something in me that refused to embrace them.” The thoughts came into his head, but he hated them. They were happening to him; they were not what he wanted.

He also heard the tempter’s other strategy: not a frontal attack, but slow erosion. “I will cool you insensibly, by degrees, by little and little... Continual rocking will lull a crying child asleep.” If loud temptation couldn’t win, the plan was to make him gradually stop caring.

Help came in pieces at first, “hints, touches, and short visits.” Then one day, travelling into the country and thinking about how hostile his heart had been towards God, he remembered that Christ had “made peace through the blood of his cross.” He saw, “again, and again, and again, that day, that God and my soul were friends by this blood.” Another time, sitting by his own fire, the promise that Jesus came to free those who “through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” hit him so hard he nearly fainted, “not with grief and trouble, but with solid joy and peace.”

He also found a very old, falling-apart copy of Martin Luther’s commentary on Galatians, and felt that it had been “written out of my heart.” Someone more than a hundred years earlier had gone through the same thing. He wasn’t the only one.

Let’s be very direct. Some people have thoughts that force their way in — violent, blasphemous, sexual or frightening — and the more they hate them, the louder they get. If that’s you, two things. First: a thought you hate and fight is not the same as a choice you made. Bunyan saw that, and so can you. Second: this is something doctors and wise pastors understand and can help with. Bunyan suffered alone for a year. You don’t have to.

One thing to do this week: if unwanted thoughts like these trouble you, tell one trusted adult this week: a parent, a pastor, a youth leader or a doctor. If they don’t, think of someone you know who seems to be carrying something heavy, and simply ask them how they’re really doing.

study_questions.answer: That something in him hated them and refused to embrace them. They came into his mind, but he did not want them.

study_questions.question: What was the tempter’s “cool you by degrees” strategy?
study_questions.answer: Not a big attack but slow erosion: to make him gradually stop caring about God, the way rocking slowly lulls a crying child to sleep.

study_questions.question: What can someone learn from this chapter if they struggle with unwanted thoughts?
study_questions.answer: That a thought you hate and fight is not a choice you have made, that others have been through the same thing, and that they should tell a trusted adult or doctor instead of suffering alone as Bunyan did.

fields.title: Sell Him
fields.body_html:
“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” — Hebrews 12:16–17 (KJV)

After that first storm, Bunyan had a season of real peace. He loved Christ, he said, with a love “as hot as fire.” He thought nothing could shake him. He was wrong. “God can tell how to abase us, and can hide pride from man. Quickly after this my love was tried to purpose.”

A new temptation arrived, and it was relentless. The thought was: sell Christ. Give him up. Swap him for anything. It came into everything he did, so that he “could neither eat my food, stoop for a pin, chop a stick, or cast mine eye to look on this, or that, but still the temptation would come, Sell Christ for this, or sell Christ for that; sell Him, sell Him.”

Sometimes it ran a hundred times in a row. He fought it so hard that his body moved, pushing with his hands and elbows, answering as fast as it came: “I will not, I will not, I will not, I will not; no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands of worlds.” It went on, he says, for about a year.

Then one morning, lying in bed, the thought came faster than ever: “Sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him.” He answered “No, no, not for thousands” at least twenty times, until he was almost out of breath. And then, exhausted, he felt this pass through his heart: “Let Him go, if He will!” and he thought he felt his heart agree.

His description of what came next is painful to read: “down I fell, as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.” He got up and walked out into a field, “like a man bereft of life,” for two hours. And a verse attached itself to him: the one at the top of this chapter, about Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal and later “found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.”

Bunyan was certain he was Esau. He had sold Christ. That verse would be with him, in his words, “all day long, all the week long, yea, all the year long.” For the next two years he believed he had committed the one sin God cannot forgive.

Before we follow him out of that field, notice two things. First: he had fought that thought for a year. He prayed against it, hated it, resisted it until he couldn’t breathe. One exhausted moment of giving way is not the same as a settled decision to walk away from Jesus. Second: the very fact that he was devastated, that he walked into a field feeling dead, shows where his heart really was. People who truly want to be rid of God don’t grieve like that.

One thing to do this week: if you’ve ever had a moment you’re sure disqualifies you, a word, a thought, a weakness, write down what you think it “proves” about you. Then ask: is this one moment, or what my heart truly wants? Keep the paper. You’ll come back to it at the end of this book.

study_questions.question: What was the “Sell Him” temptation?
study_questions.answer: A thought that came into Bunyan’s mind constantly for about a year, telling him to sell or give up Christ for anything at all. He fought it, answering “I will not” over and over.

study_questions.question: Why did Bunyan think he was like Esau?
study_questions.answer: Because after a moment of exhaustion in which he felt his heart agree, “Let Him go, if He will!”, he believed he had sold Christ the way Esau sold his birthright, and could never find repentance.

study_questions.question: What does his reaction after that morning suggest about where his heart really was?
study_questions.answer: His deep grief shows he loved Christ and did not want to lose him. People who truly want to be rid of God do not mourn like that.

fields.title: Not unto Death
fields.body_html:
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7 (KJV)

For months the Esau verse sounded in Bunyan’s head “like fetters of brass to my legs.” He started comparing his sin with the worst sinners in the Bible to see if anyone had done as badly and still been saved.

David committed adultery and arranged a murder, but that, Bunyan argued, was a sin against the law, and Christ could forgive it. Peter denied Jesus three times, which came closest; but Peter had only denied his Master, while Bunyan felt he had sold his Saviour. That left Judas. He compared himself with Judas over and over, looking for a hair’s breadth of difference. He found one: Judas acted on purpose, with deliberation, while Bunyan’s thought had come “against my prayer and strivings,” in “a fearful hurry, on a sudden.” It gave him a little relief, but only for a little while.

He did something brave: he told an older Christian everything and said he was afraid he had committed the sin against the Holy Spirit. The man “told me he thought so too.” Bunyan calls this “but cold comfort.” The man was good, but “a stranger to much combat with the devil.” Not every Christian adult will know what to say, and that’s worth remembering.

He read the story of a man named Francis Spira, who had died in despair, and it was “as salt, when rubbed into a fresh wound.” For whole days he felt his body shake. He found it hard even to pray.

One day he walked to a nearby town, sat down on a bench in the street and fell into a deep gloom. The sun seemed to grudge him light; the stones and roof tiles seemed to turn against him. Then he sighed out loud, “How can God comfort such a wretch as I?” and immediately came the answer, “as an echo doth answer a voice”: This sin is not unto death. He felt “as if I had been raised out of a grave.” If his sin was not the sin unto death, it could be forgiven, and he could pray like anyone else.

Another evening he prayed, “O Lord, I beseech thee, show me that thou hast loved me with everlasting love,” and the words came back like an echo, “I have loved thee with an everlasting love.” He went to bed at peace, and woke with it still there.

It didn’t last. The fear came back, and he says he was not fully at peace again for “well-nigh two years and an half.” The tempter told him neither God’s mercy nor Christ’s blood could help him, so it was pointless to pray. “Yet, thought I, I will pray.” His prayer is one of the bravest lines in the book:

“Lord, Satan tells me that neither Thy mercy, nor Christ’s blood, is sufficient to save my soul; Lord, shall I honour Thee most, by believing Thou wilt and canst? or him, by believing Thou neither wilt nor canst? Lord, I would fain honour Thee, by believing Thou wilt and canst.”

Under it all, one verse had spoken first, months before, as he walked by a hedge: “The blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanseth us from all sin.” All sin. Even his.

One thing to do this week: the next time you feel too bad to pray, pray anyway, using Bunyan’s line in your own words: “God, I’d rather honour you by believing you can and will forgive me, than believe the voice that says you can’t.”

study_questions.question: What happened when Bunyan told an older Christian about his fear?
study_questions.answer: The man said he thought Bunyan had committed the unforgivable sin too. Bunyan called it cold comfort and realised the man, though good, had little experience of that kind of struggle.

study_questions.question: What did Bunyan pray when he was told prayer was useless?
study_questions.answer: He asked God whether he would honour God more by believing God could and would save him, or by believing the tempter, and said he would rather honour God by believing he could and would.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that this sin was “not unto death”?
study_questions.answer: That it was not the one sin that cannot be forgiven, so Bunyan could pray, repent and come to God like any other sinner.

fields.title: Him That Cometh
fields.body_html:
“All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)

Recovery was not a straight line. Bunyan said his peace would go “in and out, sometimes twenty times a day.” He described two verses sitting in his mind like the two pans of a pair of scales: “My grace is sufficient” on one side, Esau on the other. Whichever was heavier decided his mood.

The grace verse came to him slowly. At first it was only “My grace is sufficient,” which gave him hope, but he noticed the words “for thee” were missing, and he wasn’t satisfied. Two weeks earlier he had read that verse and thrown the book down “in a pet,” sure it wasn’t big enough for him. Then one day, in a meeting of Christians, feeling as hopeless as ever, the whole thing broke in: “My grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee, my grace is sufficient for thee,” three times. Every word, he said, felt enormous: “my, and grace, and sufficient, and for thee.” He felt as if Jesus were looking down “through the tiles upon me.”

He prayed for the two verses to come at him together, so he could see which would win. A few days later they did. They “did work and struggle strangely in me for a while,” and then the Esau verse grew weak and faded, and grace won. Another verse arrived with it: “Mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”

Then came the verse at the top of this chapter, which became the one he fought hardest for in his whole life: “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” He loved the words “in no wise”: by no means, for nothing, whatever he has done. The tempter tried to say Jesus meant smaller sinners, not him. Bunyan answered, “Satan, here is in this word no such exception; but him that comes, him, any him.” He pictured it as a tug of war over the verse: “he pulled and I pulled; but, God be praised, I got the better of him.”

He also found great help in the Old Testament cities of refuge. Someone who killed a person by accident could run to one and be protected, as long as they had not acted out of hatred. Bunyan felt he was that man. He hadn’t hated Christ. He had fought that thought for a year; it had passed through his heart “in spite of my teeth.”

And finally he did the thing he had been too scared to do: he went back to the frightening verses in Hebrews and read them carefully. They “looked not so grimly on me as before.” They described people who openly, deliberately, permanently turn their backs on Christ, not a struggling believer who had lost one terrible battle and wept over it.

If a verse has been scaring you, the answer usually isn’t to avoid it. It’s to read it properly, in its context, ideally with someone wiser, next to everything else God says. Bunyan was afraid of three or four sentences. He ended up standing on one promise: in no wise cast out.

One thing to do this week: if a Bible verse frightens you, don’t skip it. Read the whole chapter around it this week, and ask a pastor or mature Christian what it means. Then write John 6:37 somewhere you’ll see it daily.

study_questions.answer: Like a pair of scales: “My grace is sufficient” on one side and the verse about Esau on the other. His peace or terror depended on which was heavier.

study_questions.question: Why did Bunyan love the words “in no wise” in John 6:37?
study_questions.answer: Because they mean by no means and for no reason, whatever a person has done. When the tempter said Jesus meant other sinners, Bunyan answered that the verse has no exception: “him, any him.”

study_questions.question: What happened when he finally read the frightening verses in Hebrews carefully?
study_questions.answer: He found they described people who openly and permanently reject Christ, not a struggling believer, and they no longer looked so grim to him.

Every word, he said, felt enormous: “my, and grace, and sufficient, and for thee.” He felt as if Jesus were looking down “through the tiles upon me.” He prayed for the two verses to come at him together, so he could see which would win. A few days later they did. They “did work and struggle strangely in me for a while,” and then the Esau verse grew weak and faded, and grace won. Another verse arrived with it: “Mercy rejoiceth against judgment.” Then came the verse at the top of this chapter, which became the one he fought hardest for in his whole life: “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” He loved the words “in no wise”: by no means, for nothing, whatever he has done. The tempter tried to say Jesus meant smaller sinners, not him. Bunyan answered, “Satan, here is in this word no such exception; but him that comes, him, any him.” He pictured it as a tug of war over the verse: “he pulled and I pulled; but, God be praised, I got the better of him.” He also found great help in the Old Testament cities of refuge. Someone who killed a person by accident could run to one and be protected, as long as they had not acted out of hatred. Bunyan felt he was that man. He hadn’t hated Christ. He had fought that thought for a year; it had passed through his heart “in spite of my teeth.” And finally he did the thing he had been too scared to do: he went back to the frightening verses in Hebrews and read them carefully. They “looked not so grimly on me as before.” They described people who openly, deliberately, permanently turn their backs on Christ, not a struggling believer who had lost one terrible battle and wept over it. If a verse has been scaring you, the answer usually isn’t to avoid it. It’s to read it properly, in its context, ideally with someone wiser, next to everything else God says. Read the whole chapter around it this week, and ask a pastor or mature Christian what it means. Then write John 6:37 somewhere you’ll see it daily.

fields.title: Thy Righteousness Is in Heaven
fields.body_html:
“But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.” — 1 Corinthians 1:30 (KJV)

Even after the storm passed, Bunyan says, “some drops did still remain.” Like someone who has been in a fire, every little noise sounded like “Fire, fire.” Any small touch hurt his tender conscience. He was better, but still jumpy, still checking whether he was really all right.

Then, one day, walking through a field, still with “some dashes on my conscience, fearing lest yet all was not right,” this sentence fell on him: Thy righteousness is in heaven. And he seemed to see, “with the eyes of my soul, Jesus Christ at God’s right hand.”

Here is what he understood in that moment, and it may be the most important thing in this book:

“I also saw, moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.”

For years Bunyan had been checking his own heart: Am I feeling faithful? Am I feeling forgiven? Am I sure enough? If he felt good, he thought he was safe. If he felt bad, he thought he was lost. That day he saw that his standing with God wasn’t inside him at all. It was in heaven, at God’s right hand, in Jesus, who does not change.

“Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed,” he wrote. He went home rejoicing. When he got home he looked for that exact sentence in his Bible and couldn’t find it, and for a moment his heart began to sink. Then he remembered the verse at the top of this chapter: Christ is “made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.” The truth was there after all.

He used a brilliant picture. Rich men, he said, carry small change in their purses, cracked coins and little silver pieces, while their real gold stays locked in a chest at home. Whatever goodness was growing in him was just the small change. “Oh, I saw my gold was in my trunk at home! In Christ, my Lord and Saviour! Now Christ was all.”

If your faith depends on how you feel about yourself today, it will go up and down with your sleep, your grades, your friendships and your hormones. Bunyan lived like that for years and nearly broke. Your bad days don’t make Jesus less righteous. Your good days don’t make him more. Your gold is at home.

One thing to do this week: every time this week you catch yourself measuring how good a Christian you feel, stop and say (silently is fine): “My righteousness is in heaven.” Count how many times you need to say it. That number tells you something.

study_questions.question: What did Bunyan realise in the field about his righteousness?
study_questions.answer: That his good or bad feelings did not make his righteousness better or worse, because his righteousness was Jesus Christ himself in heaven, who never changes.

study_questions.question: What did Bunyan mean by “my gold was in my trunk at home”?
study_questions.answer: That the goodness growing in him was like small change in a purse, while his real wealth, his righteousness, was safely kept in Christ.

study_questions.question: Why is faith based on your feelings about yourself so unstable?
study_questions.answer: Because those feelings rise and fall with ordinary things like sleep, school and friendships, but Christ’s righteousness, which actually saves, never changes.

fields.title: In Chains to Those in Chains
fields.body_html:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.” — 1 Corinthians 13:1 (KJV)

About five or six years after his awakening, the most respected members of the Bedford church noticed that Bunyan could explain the Bible well, and asked him to speak at their meetings. He was nervous and reluctant, but he did it, first in private, then travelling with others into the villages. Eventually the church prayed and fasted and called him to preach publicly. People came “by hundreds, and that from all parts.”

Here is what is surprising: he was still struggling while he did it. He describes walking to the pulpit door “full of guilt and terror,” having it lift while he preached, and then feeling as bad as ever “before I could get down the pulpit stairs.” He didn’t wait until he was fixed. And he didn’t pretend:

“I preached what I felt, what I smartingly did feel... Indeed I have been as one sent to them from the dead; I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains; and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of.”

For two years he preached mostly about sin and its danger, because that was what he knew best. As God gave him peace, his preaching changed: he talked more and more about Jesus Christ himself. He said he never meant to argue about small matters Christians disagree on; he stuck to “the word of faith and the remission of sins by the death and sufferings of Jesus.” And he loved going to “the darkest places of the country,” to people furthest from church.

He was honest about the temptations of being good at something. Sometimes people admired him, and pride crept in. What helped was the verse at the top of this chapter. A cymbal can make beautiful music, he said, but the music isn’t in the cymbal; it’s in the person playing it. A gifted person without love is just a well-played instrument. “What, thought I, shall I be proud because I am a sounding brass? Is it so much to be a fiddle?” His conclusion: “great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace.”

He also faced lies. People said he was a witch, a Jesuit, a highwayman, and that he had mistresses and even two wives. He answered calmly that God knew he was innocent, that he prayed for his accusers to repent, and that being slandered for Christ was a mark of a follower, not a disgrace.

You might be good at something: music, sport, speaking, leading, posting. Gifts are good; Bunyan says so. But they don’t prove anything about your heart, and they can quietly puff you up. And you don’t have to be finished before God uses you. Bunyan preached in chains to people in chains, and hundreds came.

One thing to do this week: name one gift you have. This week, use it once purely to serve or encourage someone else, with no credit attached. Then thank God for it, instead of quietly thanking yourself.

study_questions.answer: Because he was still struggling with guilt and fear himself while preaching, and he preached honestly about what he felt rather than pretending to be finished.

study_questions.question: What did the picture of the cymbal teach Bunyan about his gifts?
study_questions.answer: That the music comes from the player, not the instrument, so a gifted person without love is like a cymbal: useful in God’s hands but with no life of its own. He concluded that great grace with small gifts is better than great gifts without grace.

study_questions.question: How did Bunyan respond to the lies people spread about him?
study_questions.answer: He said God knew he was innocent, prayed for his accusers to repent, and treated being slandered for Christ as a mark of following him rather than a disgrace.

fields.title: Sink or Swim
fields.body_html:
“Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?” — Job 1:9 (KJV)

After about five years of preaching, Bunyan was arrested at a meeting in the countryside, before he could preach that day. England had restored its king, and preaching outside the official Church of England was now illegal. He would not promise to stop preaching or conform to the Church of England, and he was sent back to prison. When he wrote the last pages of this book, he had been there twelve years.

Prison was not only hard. Bunyan says he “never had in all my life so great an inlet into the Word of God as now.” Jesus Christ “was never more real and apparent than now.” The verses about the heavenly city and the “innumerable company of angels” in Hebrews 12 comforted him so much that he could sometimes “laugh at destruction.”

But he was honest about what hurt. Leaving his wife and children was “as the pulling the flesh from the bones,” especially his “poor blind child,” who, he wrote, “lay nearer my heart than all beside.” He imagined the child begging, cold and hungry: “I cannot now endure the wind should blow upon thee.” He felt like a man pulling his house down on his own family. And yet: “I must do it, I must do it.” He clung to God’s promise: “Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive.”

Early on, not knowing the law, he became convinced he might be hanged. For weeks God felt completely hidden. A voice asked: what if you die like this, with no comfort, no assurance? He was ashamed to think he might climb the gallows ladder “with a pale face, and tottering knees.” Then he made a decision, and these may be the bravest words he ever wrote:

“If God doth not come in, thought I, I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell, Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do; if not, I will venture for thy name.”

As soon as he decided, a verse dropped into his mind, Satan’s accusation against Job: “Doth Job fear God for nought?” The accusation was that Job only served God for what he got out of it. Bunyan realised that if he was willing to follow God with no comfort and no reward at all, that was a sign his heart was real. “I would not have been without this trial for much,” he wrote.

He wrote this book in that prison, to the people he had led to faith. He said it was like the honey Samson found inside the carcass of a lion: a temptation that roars at you at first, but once you have come through it, you find something sweet inside. He wrote plainly on purpose: “God did not play in convincing of me, the devil did not play in tempting of me, neither did I play when I sunk as into a bottomless pit... wherefore I may not play in my relating of them.”

Find the note you wrote after the “Sell Him” chapter. The man who felt shot down like a bird from a tree, who was sure he had sold Christ forever, ended up willing to jump blindfold into eternity for Jesus’ name. The grace that rescued him didn’t depend on how he felt. It still doesn’t, for you.

One thing to do this week: read the note you wrote after chapter seven. Under it, write Bunyan’s line: “Lord Jesus, if thou wilt catch me, do.” Then decide one thing you’ll do for Jesus this week whether it feels rewarding or not.

study_questions.question: Why was Bunyan in prison, and for how long when he finished this book?
study_questions.answer: For holding religious meetings outside the Church of England after that became illegal, and refusing to stop preaching or conform. He had been in prison twelve years.

study_questions.question: What was hardest about prison for Bunyan?
study_questions.answer: Being separated from his wife and children, especially his blind child, whom he loved most and feared would suffer without him.

study_questions.question: What did “Doth Job fear God for nought?” show him?
study_questions.answer: That being willing to follow God with no comfort or reward at all, even to death, was a sign his heart was sincere rather than serving God for what he could get.

fields.title: Where Sin Abounded
fields.body_html:
“Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.” — Romans 5:20 (KJV)

The title of Bunyan’s book comes from the verse above, and he calls himself “the chief of sinners,” which is what Paul called himself too. Looking back over everything, Bunyan tried to explain what it had all been for.

First, he was honest about what he thought had gone wrong. After his first deliverance, he says, he prayed only for his present troubles to go away, and never asked God to keep him from temptations still to come. From then on, he said, “I dare not, when I come before the Lord, go off my knees, until I entreat Him for help and mercy against the temptations that are to come.” And he confessed that once, during his wife’s painful early labour, he had secretly tested God: if you take away her pain tonight, I’ll know you can read my thoughts. Her pains stopped and she slept. Later, when his “Let Him go” thought came, he felt God reminding him that he really does know our secret thoughts. He should have trusted God’s word, he said, instead of putting “an if upon the all-seeingness of God.”

Second, he listed what the long struggle gave him. He could never again doubt that God is real; the doubts that had once tormented him were gone. The Bible became overwhelmingly important to him, every sentence weighed and read. He learned to grab God’s promises even when he didn’t feel their comfort, like a horse stuck in mud “flouncing” towards solid ground. “God had a bigger mouth to speak with than I had heart to conceive with,” he wrote. And he found “heights and depths in grace, and love, and mercy” he had never seen before. “Great sins to draw out great grace.”

His preface to the book is addressed to the people he had brought to faith, and it ends with advice that fits anyone reading this:

“If you have sinned against light; if you are tempted to blaspheme; if you are down in despair; if you think God fights against you; or if heaven is hid from your eyes, remember it was thus with your father, but out of them all the Lord delivered me.”

Bunyan was not a hero because he never doubted or failed. He was a mess for years. He was proud, scared, obsessive, despairing, and sure he was beyond saving. What makes his story worth telling is what God did with that mess: he didn’t throw it away. He used it to write The Pilgrim’s Progress, one of the most-read books in the English language, and this honest account that has helped struggling people for more than three hundred years.

Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. Not grace that waited for Bunyan to sort himself out. Grace that found him in the middle of a game, followed him through the field, outlasted the voices, and caught him when he jumped.

One thing to do this week: this week, pray Bunyan’s new habit: don’t just ask God to fix today’s problem; ask him to keep you through tomorrow’s temptations too. And if you know someone in despair, tell them, kindly, that one of the greatest Christian writers in history was once sure he was beyond saving.

study_questions.answer: Any two of: he could never again doubt God was real; the Bible became deeply precious to him; he learned to hold on to God’s promises even without feeling their comfort; and he saw far greater depths of God’s grace.

study_questions.answer: That however great his sin, doubt and despair were, God’s grace was greater still, and it found and held him through all of it rather than waiting for him to fix himself.
